# Impurity

250 But for one in whom this is cut off, destroyed at the root and uprooted, that person truly attains <term>samādhi</term> <gloss>mental concentration</gloss> by day and by night.
<margin>8 The Story of the Youthful Tissa; Commentary volume 3, page 357</margin>

251 There is no fire like passion, no grip like hatred, no net like delusion, and no river like craving.
<margin>9 The Story of the Five Lay-Devotees; Commentary volume 3, page 360</margin>

252 The faults of others are easy to see, but one's own are difficult to perceive. One winnows the faults of others like chaff, but hides one's own, just as a dishonest gambler hides a losing throw <note>original: "kaliṃ"; the losing side of a die in a game of chance</note>.
<margin>10 The Story of Meṇḍaka the Treasurer; Commentary volume 3, page 363</margin>

253 For one who focuses on the faults of others and is always prone to take offense, the <term>āsavas</term> <gloss>mental taints or cankers</gloss> increase. Such a person is far from the destruction of these taints.
<margin>11 The Story of the Monk who is Quick to Find Fault; Commentary volume 3, page 376</margin>

254 There is no path in the sky; there is no <term>samaṇo</term> <gloss>true ascetic</gloss> outside the Buddhist Path. Humankind delights in <term>papañca</term> <gloss>conceptual proliferation and worldly obstacles</gloss>, but the <term>Tathāgatā</term> <gloss>Thus-Gone Ones; the Buddhas</gloss> are free from these obstacles.

255 There is no path in the sky; there is no <term>samaṇo</term> <gloss>true ascetic</gloss> outside the Buddhist Path. No conditioned things are eternal; there is no instability in the Buddhas.
<margin>12 The Story of the Wanderer Subhadda; Commentary volume 3, page 377</margin>

->### XVIII THE CHAPTER ON IMPURITY: THE EIGHTEENTH<-

---

<note>Footnotes from the source manuscript regarding textual variants:</note>
1 Burmese edition: <term>kaḷi va</term> <gloss>like a losing die</gloss>. 2 Some versions read: <term>va</term> <gloss>like</gloss>.
3 Some versions read: <term>bāhiro</term> <gloss>outside</gloss>; others read: <term>bāhire</term> <gloss>in the outside</gloss>.

252 Also found in the Jātaka, volume 3, page 223.

<summary>This page contains verses 250 to 255 of the Dhammapada's Chapter on Impurity, focusing on the difficulty of recognizing one's own faults and the destructive nature of passion and craving. It emphasizes that true spiritual practice is internal and that the Buddhas are free from the instability of the conditioned world.</summary>
